questions.q: In the Meridian Logistics scenario, what did checking the Slow Request Log confirm before any configuration was touched?
options: There was no actual slowdown, and the dispatcher complaints were mistaken
The Open Incidents list view was genuinely averaging 3.8 seconds, up from a roughly 1.1-second baseline, with time concentrated in rendering and scripts rather than the database
The database query itself was the slowest part of the transaction, by far
The instance needed to be restarted to resolve the issue
questions.explain: The log turned a vague complaint into a measured, nearly 3x slowdown, and pointed toward rendering/scripts rather than the database — steering the rest of the investigation.

questions.q: Why did the four reference-field columns in the Open Incidents List Layout matter to performance?
options: Reference columns are always hidden by default and shouldn't appear in any list
They had no effect, since reference fields render identically to plain fields
They only mattered because the Vendor column was misspelled
Each required its own per-row lookup to resolve a sys_id into a displayed value, multiplied across 200-plus rows on every render
questions.explain: Four reference columns across 200-plus rows meant hundreds of extra per-row lookups on every single list render.

questions.q: What made the two UI Policies on the Incident form redundant?
options: One of the two policies was already disabled and had no effect
Both made Resolution Notes mandatory for essentially the same business reason, just checking slightly different State values, and both fired on every load regardless of the record's actual state
They governed two completely unrelated fields with no overlap at all
Both policies had "Run scripts" enabled with identical expensive scripts
questions.explain: One checked State = Resolved and the other State = Closed for the same underlying rule — a single combined condition replaces both.

questions.q: What's the honest, typical outcome of fixing both the column and UI-Policy issues in this lab, per the lesson?
options: Neither fix alone is a dramatic silver bullet, but applied across many list renders and form opens a day, the cumulative improvement is real and measurable
Removing the Vendor column alone fixes the problem completely, with no further action needed
The fixes only help a single dispatcher's session, not the list or form generally
Neither fix has any measurable effect on performance
questions.explain: Both issues are individually modest but cumulative in effect — consistent with the pattern from Lessons 2 and 3.

questions.q: Why must confirming the problem in the Slow Request Log come before reviewing the List Layout or UI Policies, rather than after or not at all?
options: It replaces the need to review the List Layout or UI Policies at all
It establishes that a real, measurable problem exists and gives an early signal of where the time is actually going, before investing effort in a specific configuration review
It is only useful after a fix has already been applied, as a final check
It has no real bearing on the order of investigation and is purely optional
questions.explain: This is the chapter's core sequence: measure and confirm first, then investigate specific likely causes guided by what the measurement showed.
